column2: FAO/ NASA Harvest Malawi Crop Cut Yield 2022
UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) & NASA Harvest, (2022). FAO/ NASA Harvest Malawi Crop Cut Yield 2022. (NASA Harvest Data Portal; V1) [data set].

The 2022 FAO/ NASA Harvest Malawi Crop Cut dataset provides sample crop cut yield data from selected maize fields across Mzimba North, Kasungu, and Balaka Districts, Malawi that represent yield variability at the national level.
UN FAO, NASA Harvest, FAO Malawi, Ministry of Agriculture Malawi

The field location and field boundary and area in hectares was collected from every identified field. From each field, two 5x5 meter crop cuts were conducted. The location of the sample crop cuts was randomly selected using the length and width measurements of the field and ensuring that the randomly generated coordinates placed the sample crop cuts within the field boundaries and that no portion of the crop cut was within 5 meters of the field edge. At the randomly generated coordinate the 5x5 meter crop cut plot were 1. measured out, 2. demarcated, 3. harvested in sequence. The maize cobs harvested from the sample crop cut plots were 1. cleaned, 2. weighed, 3. counted 4. 20 percent of the cobs were randomly selected and dekerneled to assess the kernel weight and 5. measure the moisture content of the maize kernels to calculate dry weight of the kernels. The measurements were recorded using the Survey 123 application and a farmer survey was taken at each sampled field to record qualitative information related to yield including the farmer field practices and crop condition assessment.

The objective of the sampling frame was to select 300 villages across the three selected districts (Balaka, Kasungu, Mzimba North) for the crop cut exercise that represents yield variability. For this sampling frame, we used the following datasets: Malawi Villages point layer from FAO Malawi, Malawi Admin Levels 1 (corresponding to region), 2 (to district), and 3 (to sub district) layers from GAUL, Malawi Cropland Mask 2020/2021 from NASA Harvest, and Sentinel-2 Imagery with calculated NDVI. Our first action was to select villages in Balaka, Kasungu, and Mzimba North that are surrounded by majority cropland by creating a 2-kilometer buffer around each village and sampled the 2020/2021 Malawi Cropland Mask from NASA Harvest to find the villages with at least 50% cropland in the surrounding area, to define ‘rural villages’. Then for each rural village, the current season peak NDVI (vegetation greenness) value and the 5-year average peak NDVI value were calculated, and each village was classified into High, Medium, and Low NDVI profiles using Natural Breaks (Jenk’s), compared to both all villages in Malawi and all villages in its region. Next, we randomly selected villages in each district representing each category of High, Medium and Low. We then provided the master list of 100 villages across each district to FAO Malawi for expert review and final selection. From this list FAO Malawi & NASA Harvest together selected 50 villages from each district as the final selection considering yield variability & representation, ease of access & logistics.
